old: “The hen-pheasant on the hill bridge — she knows her season! She knows her season!”
new: "The hen-pheasant on the hill bridge — she knows her season! She knows her season!"
why: Form policy: Books VI-X use curly quotes and apostrophes, I-V and XI-XX straight; normalize to straight so romanized names (Ch'i, K'ung) match byte for byte across the edition.

old: Put faithfulness and keeping your word first.
new: Put loyalty and good faith first.
why: Repeat policy: 主忠信 (I.8) recurs verbatim at IX.24 and XII.10, both rendered "Put loyalty and good faith first"; one wording for all three.

old: it unfolded everything I had taught him
new: it unfolded what I had taught him
why: 亦足以發 says only that his conduct was enough to bring out the teaching (Legge: able to illustrate); "everything" is added.

old: the salary is in there
new: the salary lies in that
why: 祿在其中矣; "in there" is chatty against the close of the saying.

old: teach the unable, and they will spur one another on
new: teach those who fall short, and they will be spurred on
why: 舉善而教不能則勸: "one another" is added and "the unable" is an awkward noun.

old: In festival, better spare than lavish.
new: In ritual, better spare than lavish.
why: 禮與其奢也寧儉: the clause is about 禮, ritual in general; "festival" comes from Legge's gloss and is not idiomatic.

old: lifts my meaning
new: draws out my meaning
why: 起予者商也: Shang rouses or brings out the Master's thought (Legge: can bring out my meaning); "lifts my meaning" is not a sense a reader carries.

old: by ritual and its deference
new: by ritual and deference
why: 禮讓 is one paired term; "its deference" is stiff.

old: And Ts'ze — what do you say of him?
new: And I, Ts'ze — what do you say of me?
why: 賜也何如: Ts'ze is Tsze-kung's own name, so he asks about himself (Legge: What do you say of me, Ts'ze?); "of him" points to a third man.

old: Where would he get unbending?
new: How could he be unbending?
why: 焉得剛; the edition's sentence is ungrammatical and trips.

old: given the name Wan — 'the cultured'?"
new: given the name Wan?"
why: Gloss policy: 何以謂之文也 asks only why he was called Wan; the meaning of the name is a note, not text (same fix at XIV.19).

old: But his time was short, and he died.
new: By ill fortune his allotted time was short, and he died.
why: Repeat policy: 不幸短命死矣 recurs verbatim at XI.6, rendered there this way; VI.2 also dropped 不幸.

old: he does not top up the rich
new: he does not make the rich richer
why: 君子周急不繼富 (Legge: does not add to the wealth of the rich); "top up" is current slang.

old: Of these he never stopped speaking.
new: Of these he spoke again and again.
why: 皆雅言也 marks them as his regular themes (Legge: frequently discoursed); "never stopped" overstates.

old: honesty without ritual is a knife
new: honesty without ritual is harshness
why: 直而無禮則絞: 絞 is harsh, biting (Legge: rudeness); the knife image is the translator's and breaks the run of abstract nouns.

old: The Fang bird does not come
new: The phoenix does not come
why: 鳳鳥不至: the same bird 鳳 is "Phoenix" at XVIII.5; "Fang" is Legge's romanization. One name for the bird.

old: Pretending to ministers when I have none
new: Pretending I have ministers when I have none
why: 無臣而為有臣; "pretending to ministers" is unidiomatic.

old: but am I dying by the side of the road?
new: but will I die by the side of the road?
why: 予死於道路乎 (Legge: shall I die upon the road?); the present progressive misreads as a question about his illness.

old: your equal in them. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to mend it.
new: your equals. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to change.
why: Repeat policy: 毋友不如己者，過則勿憚改 is verbatim I.8; match its wording. "in them" is also a gloss.

old: There are men you can study beside whom you cannot walk the Way with. There are men you can walk the Way with whom you cannot stand firm with. And there are men you can stand firm with whom you cannot weigh things with, when the rules run out.
new: Some men you can study with, but not walk the Way with. Some you can walk the Way with, but not stand firm with. Some you can stand firm with, but not weigh things with.
why: 可與共學，未可與適道… 未可與權: stacked relatives trip the ear; "when the rules run out" is a gloss on 權.

old: He was not thinking of them at all. To real thought, what is far?
new: There was no real longing in it. To one who truly longs, what is far?
why: 未之思也，夫何遠之有: 思 is longing; "them" has no antecedent (the ode says "you").

old: his face trembled toward fear
new: his face changed, as if in fear
why: 色勃如戰色 (Legge: his countenance seemed to change, and look apprehensive); the edition's phrase stops the reader.

old: he wore whatever hung from the girdle
new: he wore all the ornaments of the girdle
why: 去喪，無所不佩: he wore every ornament; "whatever" reads as indifference.

old: nor fish or meat gone off
new: nor fish or meat that had spoiled
why: 魚餒而肉敗; "gone off" is British colloquial.

old: No one can find a word to add to what his own parents and brothers say of him.
new: No one disputes what his own parents and brothers say of him.
why: 人不間於其父母昆弟之言: no one differs from his family's praise (Legge: say nothing of him different from); not that nothing can be added.

old: white scepter stone — a flaw in white jade can still be polished away; a flaw in your words, never.
new: white scepter stone.
why: Gloss policy: 南容三復白圭 says only that he repeated the ode; its content is the translator's note.

old: The man on whom slander that soaks in like water and accusations that sting like a wound in the flesh do not work — call him clear-sighted.
new: Slander that soaks in like water, accusations that sting like a wound in the flesh — the man on whom they do not work, call him clear-sighted.
why: 浸潤之譖，膚受之愬，不行焉: the subject was buried under two long modifiers; front them, as the Chinese does.

old: he lives in the pose without a doubt in his head
new: he lives in the pose and never doubts it
why: 居之不疑; "without a doubt in his head" is chatty in a careful definition.

old: gives no name that cannot be spoken to the thing
new: gives no name that cannot be rightly spoken
why: 名之必可言也 (Legge: names he uses may be spoken appropriately); "spoken to the thing" is unclear.

old: he knew how to live in a house
new: he knew how to keep a household
why: 善居室 (Legge: knew the economy of a family well).

old: Earnest, urging, and warm — that deserves the name. With his friends, earnest and urging;
new: Earnest, encouraging, and warm — that deserves the name. With his friends, earnest and encouraging;
why: 切切偲偲: 偲偲 is mutual exhortation; "urging" does not stand as an adjective.

old: called Wan — 'the cultured.'"
new: called Wan."
why: Gloss policy: 可以為文矣; the meaning of the name belongs in a note (same fix at V.15).

old: runs three ways
new: has three parts
why: 君子道者三; "Way ... three ways" is a clumsy echo.

old: human-hearted, he is free of care; wise, he is free of confusion; brave, he is free of fear.
new: human-hearted, he is never anxious; wise, never bewildered; brave, never afraid.
why: Repeat policy: 仁者不憂，知者不惑，勇者不懼 is IX.28 (order aside); use its wording.

old: cultivates himself into reverent care
new: cultivates himself with reverent care
why: 修己以敬; "into" is unidiomatic.

old: give the body to death to bring it whole
new: give up their lives to make human-heartedness whole
why: 有殺身以成仁: "it" had no clear antecedent and the famous line was obscured (Legge: sacrifice their lives to preserve their virtue complete).

old: It is finished!
new: It is hopeless!
why: Repeat policy: 已矣乎 is "It is hopeless" at V.27.

old: the professional pleaser
new: the practiced flatterer
why: 友善柔: "professional" is a modern trade word laid over a description of manner.

old: the ruler calls her FU ZAN, the Lady. She calls herself HSIAO T'UNG, this little child. The people of the state call her CHUN FU ZAN, our lord's Lady; to people of other states, they speak of her as K'WA HSIAO CHUN, our poor little prince. And the people of other states call her CHUN FU ZAN as well.
new: the ruler calls her Fu Zan, the Lady. She calls herself Hsiao T'ung, this little child. The people of the state call her Chun Fu Zan, our lord's Lady; to people of other states, they speak of her as K'wa Hsiao Chun, our poor little prince. And the people of other states call her Chun Fu Zan as well.
why: Form: Legge's all-caps typography; nowhere else does the edition set names in capitals.

old: "So there is nowhere left to go," he said. "Fine. But why must it be Kung-shan?"
new: "If there is nowhere to go, then do not go," he said. "Why must it be Kung-shan?"
why: 末之也已，何必公山氏之之也: Tsze-lu means if there is nowhere to go, then don't go (Legge: Indeed, you cannot go!); "Fine" reads as consent.

old: But don't they also say hard — so hard that grinding cannot thin it? Don't they also say white — so white that black dye cannot darken it?
new: But don't they also say: what is truly hard, grinding cannot thin? What is truly white, black dye cannot darken?
why: 不曰堅乎，磨而不磷；不曰白乎，涅而不緇; "say hard" lacks a frame and trips.

old: They can teach you how to complain.
new: They can teach you how to voice a grievance.
why: 可以怨 (Legge: regulate feelings of resentment); "complain" sounds petty.

old: Clever words and a charming face rarely go with human-heartedness.
new: Clever words and a winning face rarely keep company with human-heartedness.
why: Repeat policy: 巧言令色，鮮矣仁 is verbatim I.3; use its wording.

old: became a slave to Chau
new: became a slave to the tyrant Chau
why: 紂, last king of Yin, is spelled like the Chau dynasty (周) the Master follows; the epithet keeps them apart (same fix at XIX.20).

old: Danger, now, for men who meddle in government!
new: Danger, now, for those who serve in government!
why: 今之從政者殆而 (Legge: those who now engage in affairs of government); "meddle" adds contempt.

old: and Confucius never got his word
new: and Confucius could not speak with him
why: 不得與之言; "never got his word" is unidiomatic.

old: how would I ever get to turning away them?
new: what business have I turning others away?
why: 如之何其拒人也 (Legge: What have we to do with the putting away of others?); the edition's clause is ungrammatical.

old: and then he criticizes
new: and then he speaks against his faults
why: 信而後諫: 諫 is remonstrance with a prince; "criticizes" is office vocabulary.

old: Chau cannot have been as wicked as his name.
new: The tyrant Chau cannot have been as wicked as his name.
why: 紂之不善: the tyrant of Yin, not the Chau dynasty (周); unmarked, a reader takes it as the dynasty (same fix at XVIII.1).

old: Hold honestly to the center.
new: Hold faithfully to the center.
why: 允執其中: 允 is truly, faithfully; "honestly" reads as candor.

old: Honor the five fine things, and cast out the four ugly things. Then he is fit
new: Let him honor the five fine things and cast out the four ugly things. Then he is fit
why: 尊五美，屏四惡 has no subject; the edition shifted from "you" to "he" within the answer.
